articles.title: Designing Branching Ghost Stories: Lessons From Building Interactive Horror
articles.excerpt: Interactive fiction and horror are a natural pair. Fear depends on anticipation, and nothing builds anticipation like knowing your own choice opened the door. But branching stories are also easy to ge…
articles.body: Interactive fiction and horror are a natural pair. Fear depends on anticipation, and nothing builds anticipation like knowing your own choice opened the door. But branching stories are also easy to get wrong: too many branches and the writing thins out, too few and the reader notices the illusion. These are the design patterns I keep coming back to when writing choice-driven ghost stories, whether in Twine, Ink, a chatbot, or plain hyperlinks. Start with the ending you are afraid of Most branching stories are written forward, from the first choice outward. For horror, it works better to start from the scares. Write the two or three endings you want readers to reach: the one where they escape, the one where they almost escape, and the one where the house wins.

articles.title: I left my journal on read. Bumpy is still typing.
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady. The journal and I are in a situationship. I write two honest sentences, feel like a person with a practice,…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady . What I Built The journal and I are in a situationship. I write two honest sentences, feel like a person with a practice, and then leave it on read for a week. 🧠 My second brain is fine with that. It already stored the launch plan. The diary is the part that goes quiet, and quiet is how I lose the thread. Bumpy is how I get back to the page. Summarize journal brings the days I did write into one place, making gaps easier to notice. Daily briefing puts today’s notes next to the tasks that are due. And if I capture “write tonight” as a dated task and then pretend I am busy, Bumpy bumps me. I still have to write the paragraph. I just stop getting to pretend I forgot.

articles.excerpt: Introduction If you have ever deployed an application the traditional way - provision an EC2 instance, install a runtime, keep it patched, watch it sit idle most of the day - AWS Lambda feels almost u…
articles.body: Introduction If you have ever deployed an application the traditional way - provision an EC2 instance, install a runtime, keep it patched, watch it sit idle most of the day - AWS Lambda feels almost unfair. Lambda is AWS's serverless compute service: you upload your code, and AWS runs it for you in response to events. No servers to provision, no operating system to patch, and no paying for idle time. You are charged per request and for the exact duration your code runs, down to the millisecond. This post is for Java and Spring Boot developers.

articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built:- LazyDesk AI is a local-first, privacy-respecting desktop assistant designed to tackle one of the most universal computer headaches: the chaotic, overflowing Downloads and Desktop folders, redundant duplicate files, and unread PDF documents. Instead of sending private desktop files to external cloud AI APIs, LazyDesk AI executes all processing locally on your own machine. It pairs deterministic system utilities for file operations with Google's open-weight Gemma 3 4B (via Ollama) for document synthesis and grounded Q&A. What effort does it save?

articles.title: LazyDesk: Let AI Clean Up Your Digital Mess While You Do Absolutely Nothing
articles.excerpt: An open-source AI project for people who have better things to do than organize files. Have you ever opened your Downloads folder looking for one important PDF, only to find hundreds of files named th…
articles.body: An open-source AI project for people who have better things to do than organize files. Have you ever opened your Downloads folder looking for one important PDF, only to find hundreds of files named things like "final_v2.pdf", "final_final_revised.pdf", and "document(17).pdf"? Same problem, different day. We all know we should organize our files. We create folders, promise ourselves we'll keep everything tidy, and occasionally spend ten minutes renaming documents. Then life gets busy, the mess returns, and we start searching for files all over again. What if your computer could handle that boring work for you? That's the idea behind LazyDesk: a local AI-powered file organization assistant designed to turn digital clutter into a clean, manageable workspace.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.excerpt: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's…
articles.body: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's a still image, video, audio, or text - that "has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence" to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies , as well as restaurants' ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials. Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad … Read the full story at The Verge.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.

articles.title: Medusa's eye, Halloween fireballs and more: 5 skywatching targets to look out for this spooky season
articles.excerpt: Five spooky skywatching targets perfect for naked eye stargazing this Halloween!
articles.body: The spooky season is officially here! To celebrate, we've put together a list of five Halloween-themed skywatching targets that you can enjoy with nothing but the naked eye or binoculars and, of course, clear skies. Over millennia, the night sky has helped shape human beliefs. In return, we have imprinted our myths, stories and perceptions upon it, seeing monsters and mythology in the twinkling lights of the stars and assigning sinister aspects to innocent cosmic objects. Many of these ghostly impressions and meanings have survived to the present day. Here are a few of our favorites. The Pleiades open star cluster Don't be fooled by their beauty; the blue-white stars of the Pleiades are dripping in spooky lore.
